content.overview: Section 113 BNS incorporates the substantive offence of a Terrorist Act into India’s general penal code for the first time in history. It penalizes acts threatening the unity, integrity, sovereignty, security, or economic security of India, or intended to strike terror through lethal weaponry, hazardous materials, counterfeit currency, kidnapping, or overawing public functionaries. It establishes seven severe tiers of punishment (including capital punishment where death results) and erects a vital jurisdictional gateway in the Explanation requiring an officer not below Superintendent of Police (SP) to decide whether to register under Section 113 BNS or under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967.

It establishes seven severe tiers of punishment (including capital punishment where death results) and erects a vital jurisdictional gateway in the Explanation requiring an officer not below Superintendent of Police (SP) to decide whether to register under Section 113 BNS or under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967.
content.study:
I. HISTORICAL GENESIS & THE ORDINARY PENAL CODE CODIFICATION
Section 113 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) represents a historic watershed in Indian criminal jurisprudence. It sits in Chapter VI ("Of Offences Affecting the Human Body") directly alongside Organised Crime (s. 111) and Petty Organised Crime (s. 112).
For over 160 years, the Indian Penal Code, 1860 contained no overarching substantive offence of "Terrorism". The colonial code addressed national security purely through Chapter VI offences against the State (such as waging war under old s. 121 / s. 147 BNS or sedition under old s. 124A). Consequently, the prosecution of terrorist acts was historically restricted to emergency or specialized enactments: TADA (1987), POTA (2002), and the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967 (UAPA).

In BNS 2023, Parliament integrated the core definition of a terrorist act into the general penal code as Section 113, modernizing national penal law to address catastrophic violence, cyber-physical threats, CBRN (chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear) warfare, hostage-taking, and economic warfare targeting monetary stability. Crucially, Section 113 does not repeal UAPA 1967; the two statutes operate in parallel, governed by an explicit jurisdictional gateway in the Explanation to Section 113.

II. DECONSTRUCTION OF SECTION 113(1): THE DUAL-PRONGED TEST
To constitute a "terrorist act" under Section 113(1), the prosecution must prove two conjunctive statutory elements:
1. The Chapeau / Mens Rea (Intent or Likelihood):
   - The act must be done with the intent to threaten or likely to threaten the unity, integrity, sovereignty, security, or economic security of India; OR
   - With the intent to strike terror or likely to strike terror in the people or any section of the people in India or in any foreign country.
2. The Modus Operandi (Clauses a, b, or c):
   - Clause (a) — Destructive Means: Using bombs, dynamite, explosive or inflammable substances, firearms, lethal weapons, poisonous or noxious gases, chemicals, or biological, radioactive, nuclear or hazardous substances to cause:
     (i) death of, or injury to, any person;
     (ii) loss of, damage to, or destruction of property;
     (iii) disruption of essential supplies or services to the community;
     (iv) damage to the monetary stability of India via counterfeit currency, coin, or material;
     (v) damage or destruction of defence or Government property in India or abroad.
   - Clause (b) — Overawing Public Functionaries: Overawing by criminal force or show of criminal force, or attempting to cause or causing the death of any "public functionary" (constitutional authorities or notified functionaries).
   - Clause (c) — Hostage-Taking & Extortion of Sovereignty: Detaining, kidnapping, or abducting any person and threatening to kill or injure them in order to compel the Government of India, State Government, foreign Government, or international organization to do or abstain from doing any act.

III. THE SEVEN TIERS OF PENAL LIABILITY UNDER SUB-SECTIONS (2) TO (7)
Parliament created an exhaustive, tiered sentencing hierarchy:
1. Section 113(2)(a) — Capital / Homicide Tier: If the terrorist act results in the death of any person, the mandatory punishment is death or imprisonment for life, and a mandatory minimum fine of ₹10,00,000 (ten lakh rupees).
2. Section 113(2)(b) — Non-Homicide Principal Offence: In any other case, imprisonment for a term not less than five years extending up to life imprisonment, and a mandatory minimum fine of ₹5,00,000.
3. Section 113(3) — Inchoate Offences & Facilitation: Whoever conspires, attempts, advocates, abets, advises, incites, or knowingly facilitates a terrorist act, or engages in acts preparatory to it: 5 years to life, and fine not less than ₹5,00,000.
4. Section 113(4) — Terrorist Training Camps & Recruitment: Organising training camps or recruiting persons for terrorist acts: 5 years to life, and fine not less than ₹5,00,000.
5. Section 113(5) — Terrorist Organisation Membership: Membership in an organisation involved in a terrorist act: Imprisonment up to life, and fine.
6. Section 113(6) — Harbouring: Voluntarily harbouring or concealing an offender: 3 years to life, and fine not less than ₹5,00,000. (The Proviso creates an absolute statutory exception for the spouse of the offender).
7. Section 113(7) — Proceeds of Terrorism: Knowingly possessing property derived or acquired through a terrorist act: Imprisonment up to life, and fine.

IV. THE SP-RANK JURISDICTIONAL GATEWAY & INTERPLAY WITH UAPA 1967
The Explanation to Section 113 provides:
"Explanation.—For the removal of doubts, it is hereby declared that the officer not below the rank of Superintendent of Police shall decide whether to register the case under this section or under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967."

Critical Procedural & Forensic Implications:
1. Jurisdictional Condition Precedent: An ordinary Station House Officer (SHO / Inspector) lacks statutory competence to unilaterally register an FIR under Section 113 BNS. The decision whether to invoke Section 113 BNS or UAPA 1967 must be taken by an officer not below the rank of Superintendent of Police (SP) or Deputy Commissioner of Police (DCP). An FIR registered under Section 113 without SP concurrence is procedurally defective.
2. Dual-Track Comparison (BNS s. 113 vs UAPA 1967):
   - Forum: Section 113 BNS is tried before the regular Court of Session under the BNSS. UAPA offences are tried before Special Courts designated under the National Investigation Agency Act, 2008.
   - Bail Regime: Section 113 BNS is governed by the regular bail provisions of Section 480 and Section 483 BNSS (subject to the severity of life/death sentences). UAPA contains the stringent twin-conditions statutory bar under Section 43D(5), where bail must be denied if the accusation appears prima facie true (NIA v. Zahoor Ahmad Shah Watali (2019) 5 SCC 1).
   - Investigation Remand: Section 113 BNS is governed by Section 187 BNSS (maximum 90 days total remand, with police custody in parts during the initial 60 days). UAPA Section 43D(2) permits extension of investigation detention up to 180 days.

V. EVIDENCE, CURRENCY FORENSICS & ARTICLE 20(1) TRANSITION
1. Counterfeit Currency Forensics: Under Explanation (b), counterfeit Indian currency requires examination and declaration by an authorised or notified forensic authority certifying that the currency imitates or compromises key security features.
2. Digital Evidence under Section 63 BSA: Cyber-terrorist communications (dark web forums, PGP-encrypted emails, Telegram broadcast channels, crypto-wallets) are secondary electronic evidence requiring mandatory Section 63(4) BSA certification.
3. Article 20(1) Non-Retrospectivity: Section 113 BNS cannot be applied retrospectively to acts committed prior to 1 July 2024. Pre-July 2024 acts must be prosecuted under UAPA 1967 or IPC Section 121.

sections.heading: The legal rule
sections.body:
113. Terrorist act.—(1) Whoever does any act with the intent to threaten or likely to threaten the unity, integrity, sovereignty, security, or economic security of India or with the intent to strike terror or likely to strike terror in the people or any section of the people in India or in any foreign country,—
(a) by using bombs, dynamite or other explosive substance or inflammable substance or firearms or other lethal weapons or poisonous or noxious gases or other chemicals or by any other substance (whether biological, radioactive, nuclear or otherwise) of a hazardous nature or by any other means of whatever nature to cause or likely to cause,—
(i) death of, or injury to, any person or persons; or
(ii) loss of, or damage to, or destruction of, property; or
(iii) disruption of any supplies or services essential to the life of the community in India or in any foreign country; or
(iv) damage to, the monetary stability of India by way of production or smuggling or circulation of counterfeit Indian paper currency, coin or of any other material; or
(v) damage or destruction of any property in India or in a foreign country used or intended to be used for the defence of India or in connection with any other purposes of the Government of India, any State Government or any of their agencies; or
(b) overawes by means of criminal force or the show of criminal force or attempts to do so or causes death of any public functionary or attempts to cause death of any public functionary; or
(c) detains, kidnaps or abducts any person and threatening to kill or injure such person or does any other act in order to compel the Government of India, any State Government or the Government of a foreign country or an international or inter-governmental organisation or any other person to do or abstain from doing any act,
commit a terrorist act.
Explanation.—For the purpose of this sub-section,—
(a) “public functionary” means the constitutional authorities or any other functionary notified in the Official Gazette by the Central Government as public functionary;
(b) “counterfeit Indian currency” means the counterfeit currency as may be declared after examination by an authorised or notified forensic authority that such currency imitates or compromises with the key security features of Indian currency.
(2) Whoever commits a terrorist act shall,—
(a) if such offence has resulted in the death of any person, be punished with death or imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine;
(b) in any other case, be punished with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than five years but which may extend to imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine.
(3) Whoever conspires or attempts to commit, or advocates, abets, advises or incites, directly or knowingly facilitates the commission of a terrorist act or any act preparatory to the commission of a terrorist act, shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than five years but which may extend to imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine.
(4) Whoever organises or causes to be organised any camp or camps for imparting training in terrorist act, or recruits or causes to be recruited any person or persons for commission of a terrorist act, shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than five years but which may extend to imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine.
(5) Any person who is a member of an organisation which is involved in terrorist act, shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine.
(6) Whoever voluntarily harbours or conceals, or attempts to harbour or conceal any person knowing that such person has committed a terrorist act shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than three years but which may extend to imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine:
Provided that this sub-section shall not apply to any case in which the harbour or concealment is by the spouse of the offender.
(7) Whoever knowingly possesses any property derived or obtained from commission of any terrorist act or acquired through the commission of any terrorist act shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine.
Explanation.—For the removal of doubts, it is hereby declared that the officer not below the rank of Superintendent of Police shall decide whether to register the case under this section or under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967 (37 of 1967).

sections.heading: Provenance, Legislative Objective & Codification in Ordinary Penal Law
sections.body:
Section 113 BNS represents the first time in Indian legal history that the substantive offence of a Terrorist Act is codified inside the general penal code.
Historically, terrorism was prosecuted exclusively under special enactments (TADA, POTA, UAPA 1967) because the IPC 1860 only contained traditional state-security offences like waging war (s. 121) or sedition (s. 124A).
Section 113 modernizes penal law to tackle CBRN weapons, infrastructure destruction, cyber-economic warfare, and hostage-taking within Chapter VI of the Sanhita.
Section 113 operates in tandem with UAPA 1967 without repealing it, providing the state with a unified statutory weapon inside the regular criminal justice machinery.

sections.heading: Textual Anatomy of Section 113(1): Chapeau, Economic Security & Modalities
sections.body:
The Chapeau requires proof of specific intent or likelihood: threatening the unity, integrity, sovereignty, security, or economic security of India, or striking terror in the populace in India or abroad.
Clause (a) enumerates lethal means: explosives, firearms, CBRN materials, or hazardous substances causing death/injury, property destruction, or essential service disruption.
Economic Warfare Codified: Clause (a)(iv) explicitly incorporates damage to the monetary stability of India through counterfeit currency, coin, or material as a terrorist act.
Clauses (b) and (c) cover overawing or killing public functionaries, and hostage-taking or abduction to coerce sovereign Governments or international bodies.

sections.heading: The Seven Tiers of Liability: Sub-sections (2) to (7) & Spousal Exception
sections.body:
Section 113(2)(a) (Homicide Tier): If the act results in death, the mandatory punishment is death or imprisonment for life, and a mandatory minimum fine of ₹10,00,000.
Section 113(2)(b) (Non-Homicide Tier): In all other cases, imprisonment from 5 years to life, and fine not less than ₹5,00,000.
Inchoate and preparatory liability: Sub-sections (3) and (4) penalize conspiracy, attempt, abetment, incitement, facilitation, training camps, and recruitment with 5 years to life.
Sub-sections (5)-(7) penalize membership in terrorist organisations, harbouring (with an absolute statutory exception for the spouse of the offender), and possession of terrorist proceeds.

sections.heading: The SP-Rank Registration Gateway: Explanation to s. 113 vs UAPA 1967
sections.body:
The Explanation creates an express statutory checkpoint: only an officer not below the rank of Superintendent of Police (SP) can decide whether to register a case under Section 113 BNS or under UAPA 1967.
Unilateral registration of Section 113 BNS by a Station House Officer without SP approval is procedurally defective and subject to quashing under Section 528 BNSS.
Bail contrast: Section 113 BNS is governed by regular Sessions Court bail under Section 480/483 BNSS; UAPA 1967 imposes the stringent Section 43D(5) statutory bail bar (Zahoor Watali doctrine).
Remand contrast: Section 113 BNS follows Section 187 BNSS (90 days max, police custody in parts during initial 60 days); UAPA Section 43D(2) permits detention up to 180 days.

sections.heading: Evidentiary Proof (BSA ss. 63, 104), Currency Forensics & Article 20(1) Bounds
sections.body:
Forensic Currency Requirement: Under Explanation (b), counterfeit currency charges require a formal report from an authorized forensic authority certifying compromise of security features.
Digital Forensics under Section 63 BSA: PGP emails, dark web servers, encrypted Telegram channels, and cryptocurrency transaction ledgers must strictly satisfy Section 63(4) certification (Arjun Panditrao Khotkar (2020)).
Article 20(1) Non-Retrospectivity: Section 113 BNS cannot be applied retrospectively to acts committed prior to 1 July 2024; pre-commencement acts must be tried under UAPA or IPC waging war.
Trial Advocacy: Scrutinize the SP approval record, forensic currency reports, and digital evidence certifications to challenge Section 113 indictments at the threshold.

examples.title: Economic Warfare — Mass Counterfeit Currency Smuggling under Section 113(1)(a)(iv)
examples.body: A cross-border syndicate smuggles ₹50 crore of high-quality counterfeit Indian currency notes into India via maritime routes. The forensic report from the Security Printing and Minting Corporation confirms that the notes replicate the watermarks, security threads, and optically variable ink of genuine currency to compromise monetary stability. Accused T is intercepted with consignments. Under Section 113(1)(a)(iv) BNS read with Explanation (b), damaging India’s monetary stability through counterfeit currency is a terrorist act. Because no death resulted, T is prosecuted under Section 113(2)(b) BNS, facing imprisonment from five years to life and a minimum fine of ₹5,00,000.

examples.title: Section 113 Indictment Defective — Absence of Mandatory SP-Rank Approval
examples.body: Following a violent scuffle at a toll plaza where country-made crude crackers were thrown, a local police Sub-Inspector registers an FIR under Section 113 BNS for a terrorist act. The accused moves the High Court under Section 528 BNSS. The record reveals that the Sub-Inspector registered the FIR directly without submitting the file or obtaining the written decision of an officer of Superintendent of Police (SP) rank as commanded by the Explanation to Section 113 BNS. The High Court holds the registration under Section 113 void for want of statutory competence and directs alteration of the FIR to ordinary penal provisions under Section 115/125 BNS.

hypotheticals.question: As Senior Counsel, analyse whether K can be indicted under Section 113 BNS for disruption of essential supplies/services through cyber means, and examine the bail prospects under BNSS Section 483 vs UAPA Section 43D(5).
hypotheticals.analysis:
1. Substantive Maintainability of Section 113 BNS:
   - Section 113(1)(a) explicitly criminalizes the use of hazardous substances "or by any other means of whatever nature" to cause "disruption of any supplies or services essential to the life of the community in India".
   - Planting ransomware to shut down an electric grid powering hospitals and military installations threatens the sovereignty and security of India, satisfying the chapeau of Section 113(1).
   - While Section 66F of the IT Act penalizes cyber terrorism, Section 113 BNS is a comprehensive general penal provision that operates concurrently; the special law does not bar prosecution under BNS where essential services are crippled.
   - K’s role in planting malware constitutes conspiracy, facilitation, and preparatory acts under Section 113(3) BNS, punishable with 5 years to life imprisonment.
2. Compliance with the SP-Rank Gateway:
   - The case was formally evaluated and registered with the written approval of the Superintendent of Police, strictly satisfying the mandatory jurisdictional condition precedent enacted in the Explanation to Section 113 BNS.
3. The Bail Regime Contrast (BNSS vs UAPA):
   - Because the SP exercised discretion to register under Section 113 BNS rather than UAPA 1967, the stringent statutory bail bar under Section 43D(5) UAPA does NOT apply.
   - Bail is governed by Section 483 BNSS before the Sessions Court or High Court. While the gravity of crippling state infrastructure creates a formidable hurdle under regular discretionary bail principles, the accused is not subject to the absolute statutory freeze of Watali (2019).
4. Evidentiary Scrutiny under Section 63 BSA:
   - Server log files, malware binaries, and Bitcoin blockchain transaction records must strictly comply with Section 63(4) BSA certification with cryptographic hashes.

misconceptions.trap: Any police officer can register an FIR for a Terrorist Act under Section 113 BNS.
misconceptions.correction: The Explanation to Section 113 explicitly mandates that an officer not below the rank of Superintendent of Police (SP) shall decide whether to register the case under Section 113 BNS or under UAPA 1967. Registration by a lower-ranked officer without SP approval is procedurally ultra vires.

misconceptions.trap: Section 113 BNS incorporates the stringent bail bar under Section 43D(5) of UAPA 1967.
misconceptions.correction: Section 113 BNS is an offence under the general penal code and is governed by regular bail provisions under Section 480 and Section 483 BNSS. The statutory restriction under Section 43D(5) UAPA does not apply to Section 113 BNS unless UAPA provisions are also charged.

misconceptions.trap: A spouse who conceals or harbours a terrorist offender is liable under Section 113(6) BNS.
misconceptions.correction: The Proviso to Section 113(6) BNS explicitly creates an absolute statutory exemption: "Provided that this sub-section shall not apply to any case in which the harbour or concealment is by the spouse of the offender."

cases.name: National Investigation Agency v. Zahoor Ahmad Shah Watali
cases.holding: Held that in anti-terror prosecutions under UAPA, the court cannot engage in a mini-trial or evaluate probative weight at the bail stage; bail must be refused if the prosecution material, taken at face value, establishes a prima facie case. This highlights the procedural contrast with Section 113 BNS bail under the BNSS.
cases.relevance: Lead precedent contrasting the stringent UAPA bail standard with regular Section 113 BNS bail adjudications.

cases.name: Hitendra Vishnu Thakur v. State of Maharashtra
cases.holding: Held that every violent act or public disturbance cannot be labeled as terrorism; a terrorist act requires the distinct intention or likelihood to strike terror or destabilize the state, distinct from ordinary criminal violence.
cases.relevance: Authoritative benchmark for distinguishing ordinary violence from Section 113 BNS terrorist acts.

cases.name: Arjun Panditrao Khotkar v. Kailash Kushanrao Gorantyal
cases.holding: Reaffirmed the mandatory requirement of a certificate for electronic evidence under Section 65B of the 1872 Act (now s. 63 BSA), which is essential in cyber and digital terrorism prosecutions.
cases.relevance: Mandatory standard for electronic and cyber forensic evidence tendered under Section 113 BNS.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Prepare an IRAC Legal Case Brief on Section 113 BNS (Terrorist Act), analyzing the chapeau requirements, the seven punishment tiers, the SP-rank registration gateway, and the procedural interplay with UAPA 1967.
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
I. ISSUE & JURISDICTIONAL THRESHOLD
Whether an act causing widespread destruction, loss of life, or damage to economic security satisfies the statutory ingredients of a Terrorist Act under Section 113 BNS, and whether the FIR was lawfully registered pursuant to the decision of an officer not below the rank of Superintendent of Police. Forum: Court of Session under the First Schedule of BNSS.

II. GOVERNING RULE & STATUTORY ANATOMY
1. The Chapeau / Mental State: Act done with intent or likelihood to threaten unity, integrity, sovereignty, security, or economic security of India, or strike terror in the people in India or abroad.
2. The Modus: Clause (a) lethal weapons, explosives, CBRN agents, property destruction, or counterfeit currency damaging monetary stability; Clause (b) overawing or killing public functionaries; Clause (c) hostage-taking and abduction.
3. Seven Sentencing Tiers: Section 113(2)(a) capital punishment/life where death results; Section 113(2)(b) 5 years to life; Section 113(3)-(4) inchoate offences and training; Section 113(5)-(7) membership, harbouring (spousal exception), and proceeds of terrorism.
4. The SP Gateway: Explanation to Section 113 mandates that an officer not below SP rank must decide whether to register under Section 113 BNS or UAPA 1967.

III. APPLICATION TO FACTUAL DISPUTE
- Step 1: Verify the registration order. Check whether the file contains the written decision of an SP/DCP approving Section 113 registration. If missing, move for quashing or alteration of charges.
- Step 2: Test mens rea under Hitendra Vishnu Thakur (1994). If the act was driven by private rivalry rather than striking terror or destabilizing sovereignty, seek alteration to ordinary homicide (s. 101) or hurt (s. 115).
- Step 3: For counterfeit currency, inspect forensic report verifying compromise of security features under Explanation (b).
- Step 4: Electronic evidence (chats, server logs) must satisfy Section 63(4) BSA certification.

IV. CONCLUSION & OPERATIVE ADVICE
Advise counsel to challenge any unilateral FIR registered by an SHO without SP sanction under the Explanation to Section 113. Emphasize that unlike UAPA Section 43D(5), Section 113 BNS is governed by regular Sessions Court bail under Section 483 BNSS, where parity and delay in trial can be forcefully argued.
questionsAndAnswers.explanation: Senior Counsel IRAC brief on Section 113 BNS terrorist act codification and procedural dynamics.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Draft comprehensive Written Submissions before the High Court under Section 528 BNSS challenging an FIR registered under Section 113 BNS by a Station House Officer without the statutory decision of an officer of Superintendent of Police rank.
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
IN THE HIGH COURT OF JUDICATURE AT [JURISDICTION]
CRIMINAL MISCELLANEOUS PETITION NO. [____] OF 202[ ]
(UNDER SECTION 528 OF THE BHARATIYA NAGARIK SURAKSHA SANHITA, 2023)

IN THE MATTER OF:
[PETITIONER NAME]                                           ... PETITIONER
VERSUS
1. STATE OF [STATE]
2. STATION HOUSE OFFICER, POLICE STATION [NAME]             ... RESPONDENTS

WRITTEN SUBMISSIONS ON BEHALF OF THE PETITIONER CHALLENGING ILLEGAL INVOCATION OF SECTION 113 BNS WITHOUT MANDATORY SP-RANK APPROVAL

MOST RESPECTFULLY SHOWETH:

I. STATEMENT OF RELEVANT FACTS & PROCEDURAL PROVENANCE
1. The Petitioner stands implicated in FIR No. [___] dated [Date], registered at Police Station [Name] under Section 113(1) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS), and Section 351 BNS.
2. The FIR was registered on the complaint of a municipal officer alleging that during an anti-encroachment drive, the Petitioner ignited a cylinder and threatened the demolition team.
3. The FIR was registered directly by Respondent No. 2 (a Sub-Inspector / SHO) without placing the matter before or obtaining the decision of any officer of the rank of Superintendent of Police.

II. PATENT BREACH OF THE MANDATORY JURISDICTIONAL GATEWAY
4. The Explanation to Section 113 BNS enacts an explicit, statutory jurisdictional limitation:
   "Explanation.—For the removal of doubts, it is hereby declared that the officer not below the rank of Superintendent of Police shall decide whether to register the case under this section or under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967."
5. Parliament consciously entrusted this sensitive discretionary power exclusively to senior supervisory officers of the rank of Superintendent of Police (SP) or Deputy Commissioner of Police (DCP), with the specific legislative objective of preventing misuse by subordinate police officers.
6. Respondent No. 2 possessed zero statutory competence to register an FIR under Section 113 BNS. The registration is ultra vires, void ab initio, and an abuse of the process of law.

III. THE ALLEGED ACT DOES NOT CONSTITUTE A TERRORIST ACT
7. In Hitendra Vishnu Thakur v. State of Maharashtra (1994) 4 SCC 602, the Supreme Court ruled that every violent dispute or public resistance to authority cannot be branded as terrorism.
8. The dispute was a localized municipal confrontation. There was zero intent or likelihood to threaten the unity, integrity, sovereignty, or economic security of India, or to strike terror in the general populace.
9. Slapping Section 113 BNS onto a municipal dispute was done maliciously to deprive the Petitioner of bail.

IV. PRESERVATION OF INHERENT JURISDICTION UNDER SECTION 528 BNSS
10. Under Section 528 BNSS (retaining the inherent powers of the High Court), this Hon’ble Court possesses the duty to quash charges that are patently without jurisdiction and prevent the harassment of citizens.

PRAYER
Wherefore, in light of the above facts, statutory scheme, and binding authorities, it is respectfully prayed that this Hon’ble Court may graciously be pleased to:
(a) Partially quash FIR No. [___] insofar as it invokes Section 113 BNS;
(b) Direct that the investigation proceed, if at all, under ordinary penal provisions; and
(c) Grant interim protection against arrest to the Petitioner.

FILED BY:
[COUNSEL FOR THE PETITIONER]
ADVOCATE

learningObjectives: Master the historic codification of a Terrorist Act within India's general penal code under BNS s. 113.
Analyze the substantive chapeau: acts threatening unity, integrity, sovereignty, security, or economic security of India, or terrorizing the public.
Examine the seven tiers of liability, including capital punishment where death results.
Understand the procedural gateway under the Explanation requiring an officer not below Superintendent of Police (SP) to determine registration under BNS vs UAPA.
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 113 incorporates the substantive offence of a Terrorist Act into general criminal law, penalizing any act done with intent to threaten or likely to threaten the unity, integrity, sovereignty, security, or economic security of India, or with intent to strike terror in the people, through bombs, dynamite, lethal weapons, biological/chemical substances, counterfeit currency, kidnapping, or overawing public functionaries.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Integrates counter-terrorism into ordinary criminal law while establishing strict institutional filters to safeguard against improper invocation.
statutoryFramework: Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body, BNS s. 113 (historic new provision in BNS 2023).

Sub-section (1): Substantive definition — acts threatening national integrity, sovereignty, or economic security, or striking terror using lethal weaponry, explosives, biological agents, or high-denomination counterfeit currency.
Sub-section (2)(a): Homicide tier — if death results: punishable with death or imprisonment for life, and fine.
Sub-section (2)(b): Other cases — imprisonment not less than five years extending to life, and fine.
Sub-sections (3)-(6): Conspiracy, organizing camps, recruiting, and harboring (excluding spouses).
Explanation: Mandates that an officer not below the rank of Superintendent of Police (SP) shall decide whether to register under Section 113 BNS or the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967.
essentialIngredients: An act was committed with intent to threaten or likely to threaten the unity, integrity, sovereignty, security, or economic security of India; OR with intent to strike terror in the people.
The act was done using bombs, dynamite, lethal weapons, poisonous gases, radioactive/nuclear substances, counterfeit currency, or by kidnapping/hostage-taking.
For sub-section (2)(a): The act resulted in the death of any person.
Registration decision: Approved by an officer not below the rank of Superintendent of Police.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 113 marks the first time that terrorism is substantively defined within India's basic penal code, rather than solely in special security enactments like UAPA. The provision adopts an expansive definition encompassing conventional violence (explosives, lethal firearms, biological weapons) as well as modern warfare such as attacks on critical infrastructure and damage to the monetary stability of India through large-scale counterfeit currency. If a terrorist act results in death, sub-section (2)(a) mandates death or life imprisonment. Ancillary provisions penalize conspiring, training camps, recruiting, and harboring (with an express exception for spouses). To prevent abuse and harmonize with UAPA, the Explanation creates a vital jurisdictional gateway: an officer not below the rank of Superintendent of Police (SP) must independently determine whether the case is registered under Section 113 BNS or under UAPA 1967.
examples: Teaching example (Bombing public transport): An operative plants an explosive device on a public metro train, killing twelve passengers, with the aim of striking terror and coercing the government. The act satisfies s. 113(1) and is punished under s. 113(2)(a) with death or life imprisonment.

Teaching example (Economic terrorism via counterfeit notes): A network imports crores of high-grade counterfeit Indian currency designed to destabilize the banking system. This falls under s. 113(1) as an act threatening the economic security of India.
distinctions: Section 113 BNS vs UAPA 1967: Section 113 incorporates the substantive offence into general penal law; UAPA provides specialized investigative procedures, detention limits, and scheduled organization bans. The SP decides the forum under the Explanation.
Terrorist Act (s. 113) vs Murder (s. 101): Murder requires intent against individuals; a terrorist act requires intent to threaten sovereignty, security, or terrorize the public at large.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether a group that took passengers hostage at an airport demanding the release of imprisoned extremists can be prosecuted under s. 113.
Rule: Detaining or kidnapping any person and threatening to kill them in order to compel the Government to do any act constitutes a terrorist act under BNS s. 113(1).
Application: The hostages were taken to coerce government action through terror.
Conclusion: The offenders are liable under BNS s. 113.

shortAnswer: Identify BNS s. 113 as the first general penal codification of terrorist acts.
List mens rea prongs: threatening sovereignty/security or terrorizing public.
State punishment: death or life imprisonment if death results; min 5 years to life otherwise.
Note SP-rank decision gateway in the Explanation.

The economic security dimension (counterfeit currency, critical infrastructure).
Sentencing tiers and ancillary offences (conspiracy, harboring).
sixteenMark: Comprehensive analysis of counter-terrorism jurisprudence in general penal law.
Detailed dissection of Section 113(1) chapeau and modalities of execution.
Harmonization with Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967 and the SP-rank gateway.
Constitutional safeguards: procedural fairness, bail parameters, and Article 20/21.

keyTakeaways: First general penal code provision defining terrorist acts in India.
Covers physical terrorism and economic terrorism (counterfeit currency).
Punishable with death or life imprisonment where death results.
Requires an officer not below Superintendent of Police (SP) to determine registration.
